newsitem.title: FRANCE: Top French body queries proposed immigration law.
newsitem.headline: Top French body queries proposed immigration law.

text.p: France's Council of State has warned the government that part of proposed new legislation to curb illegal immigration may be unconstitutional, the newspaper Le Monde said on Tuesday.

The daily said the Council, which reviews draft laws, had told the government in a note that part of a bill parliament began debating on Tuesday may "infringe on the personal freedoms and private lives of those offering shelter (to foreigners)".
A Council spokeswoman confirmed to Reuters that the body had studied the proposed legislation but would not give details of its comments.

Le Monde said the Council was challenging conditions laid down in the proposed legislation for granting visas to nationals of third world states who stayed in private homes while on short-term visits to France.
Opponents of immigration say hundreds of thousands of foreigners have entered France on such short-term visas but failed to leave and have became illegal immigrants.
The new law would allow mayors to ask police to verify if a visitor had left a private home when his visa expired.

Le Monde said the government had chosen to ignore the Council's non-binding advice that this was unconstitutional. But experts said individuals may later take the governmment to court over the issue if the legislation becomes law.
The new legislation is part of efforts by tough Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre to curb illegal immigration to France where there are about a million illegals among five million foreigners.
The illegal migrant issue led to nationwide controversy last summer when police forcibly evicted more than 200 Africans, mostly illegal immigrants, from their refuge in a Paris church.
Magistrates later thwarted orders expelling most of them and the new laws sought by Debre would prevent a repeat of the situation.
Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme rightist National Front, backed by about 15 percent of the electorate, wants to expel millions of foreigners, including those legally resident.
Rights activists accuse Debre of lacking sensitivity while ultra-leftists want Paris to offer blanket asylum to all foreigners now living in France.
Communist parliamentarian Andre Gerin said in the debate that the proposed new law would have "grave consequences on individual freedoms and fundamental rights".
Debre replied: "The loss of control over immigration would result in considerable dangers for the smooth integration of foreigners (legally in France) and for the stability of our society."
Another proposed change in current laws would double to two years the period required for the foreign spouse of a French national to obtain permanent residency rights.

Police officials say this will halt the traffic in fake weddings where foreigners offer money to poor French people to marry them, allowing them to enter the country legally, then divorce and bring their own families to France.
A chartered Romanian airliner on Tuesday flew home 51 Romanians expelled for lack of a residence permit or for disturbing the peace, the Interior Ministry said.

It was the 23rd such group expulsion since the centre-right government took office 19 months ago, pledging a crackdown on clandestine immigration, the ministry said. More than 20,000 illegal immigrants have been expelled during that period.
